analysis.one_liner: Bans coal companies from self-insuring mine cleanup, requiring real bonds so taxpayers aren't left with reclamation costs.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with 41 House sponsors and no hearing or vote, leaving coal companies free to keep self-bonding their cleanup obligations.
analysis.plain_summary: Under a practice called self-bonding, a coal company with good financials can skip buying cleanup insurance or posting cash, and simply promise it will reclaim the mined land itself. If the company later goes bankrupt, the promise is worthless and the cleanup bill can fall to taxpayers. This bill would prohibit the federal Office of Surface Mining and state regulators from accepting any new self-bonds, force existing self-bonds and corporate bonds to be replaced with surety or collateral bonds, block coal assets from being posted as collateral, and let regulators count executive pay toward a bond. It died without a hearing or vote in the House Natural Resources Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers at every level, who would no longer be the backstop when a coal company goes bankrupt before reclaiming its mines, and residents of coal communities who would see land actually restored instead of abandoned.

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars OSMRE and state regulatory authorities from accepting any new self-bonds for coal reclamation, so cleanup promises can no longer rest on a company's own word about its financial strength [S2].
Existing self-bonds and corporate bonds must be converted to surety or collateral bonds, replacing unsecured promises with actual third-party backing [S2].
Real property posted as collateral cannot include the coal mine itself, coal processing facilities, or waste sites — the very assets most likely to be worthless after a bankruptcy [S3].
The Interior Secretary may count executives' salaries and bonuses as bond collateral, making it harder for a company to shield its own pay while shifting cleanup risk [S3].

The bill requires new rules limiting how much reclamation business any one surety company can hold and how much collateral and cash it must hold, so the insurance backing the cleanup does not fail too [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal mining companies, which would pay surety premiums or post real collateral instead of self-bonding for free; those costs could pressure margins at financially weak operators and, in principle, be passed into coal prices and mining jobs.

drawbacks.text: Ending self-bonding converts a free promise into an ongoing expense for coal operators, and the added premium and collateral costs could strain already-weak companies, with job effects in coal-dependent regions [S2].

The bill restricts collateral in detail — banning coal, mines, processing facilities, waste sites, and low-value mining equipment from being posted [S3] — rules that give regulators real discretion and could be litigated or gamed by operators and sureties alike.

Existing corporate surety bonds would have to be modified or replaced within a year of the new rules [S3], an administrative burden on both mining companies and the surety industry during a period of coal-industry bankruptcies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is small and ongoing bonding costs for coal operators against avoiding large, contingent cleanup bills that fall on taxpayers when companies fail — a risk that was live in 2015-16 as major coal producers went through bankruptcy. The main honest objection is the burden on struggling coal operators and their workers, though cleanup costs exist either way; the bill's main design choice is who carries them.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, where it sat until the 114th Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Matt Cartwright introduced the bill on June 16, 2016, with 35 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Natural Resources on the day of introduction [S5].
One week later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, the last action of any kind on the bill [S5].
The bill never received a committee hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal companies came out ahead: they kept the ability to self-bond, avoiding surety premiums and collateral requirements, while taxpayers kept carrying the contingent risk of paying for mine cleanup after a bankruptcy.

sides.party_line_note: All 41 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Natural Resources Committee took no action beyond the initial referral.

industries.note: Self-bonding let operators avoid paying for cleanup coverage by promising their own financial strength; the bill ends that option, so cleanup liability shifts back onto the companies rather than sitting with taxpayers when a firm fails. Operators' interest in keeping free self-bonding ran directly against the taxpayer backstop.

The bill creates a large market by requiring every self-bond to be replaced with a surety or collateral bond, while simultaneously subjecting sureties to new limits on concentration, reinsurance, and capital [S3].

Federal and state governments absorbed reclamation costs when self-bonded operators went bankrupt; the bill removes that contingent liability. Listed because the status quo that survived the bill's death left this exposure in place.
